record.paper_title: Open problems on Steiner trees and maximal distance minimizers
record.original_question: Can one construct a nonplanar example of a unique full Steiner tree with infinitely many branching points?

evidence.quote: Question 2.14. Can one construct a non-planar example of a unique full Steiner tree with infinitely many branching points?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
A Steiner tree for a closed set $A \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ (called the terminal set) is a connected set $S \supseteq A$ of minimal one-dimensional Hausdorff measure $\mathcal{H}^1(S)$ among all connected sets containing $A$. A Steiner tree is called full if every terminal point is a leaf (an endpoint) of $S$. A branching point of $S$ is a point at which three edges meet; in Euclidean Steiner trees every branching point has degree exactly $3$ with three adjacent segments meeting at pairwise angles $2\pi/3$ and lying in a common plane. A Steiner tree $S$ for $A$ is called unique if it is the only connected set of minimal $\mathcal{H}^1$-measure containing $A$. The tree $S$ is called planar if $S$ is contained in some affine $2$-plane in $\mathbb{R}^d$, and nonplanar otherwise.

Question: Does there exist a closed set $A \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ (for some $d \geq 3$) admitting a unique full Steiner tree $S$ such that $S$ is nonplanar and has infinitely many branching points?
artifact.status_search_result: The problem is posed as an open question in a recent (2025) collection of open problems on Steiner trees. Known explicit constructions of Steiner trees with infinitely many branching points (e.g., the Paolini–Stepanov–Teplitskaya 2015 example) are all planar; no nonplanar example is known.

status_evidence.claim: Existing infinite-branching examples are planar, so the nonplanar case remains unresolved.
